Step-by-Step Audio Guided Tour: Art Institute of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA - Museum Tour
Tour-Category: museum

Stop 1: The Great Wave of Kanagawa

Coordinates: 41.8781, -87.6298

Museum Information:

The museum is open daily except Tuesday, 11:00 to 5:00. Admission is 25 dollars for adults; under-14s go free.

Orientation: You are about to explore the Art Institute of Chicago in Chicago. These diverse works span continents and centuries, united in their exploration of human emotion and experience. At The Great Wave of Kanagawa, you will see Hokusai’s celebrated Thirty-Six Views woodblock print series. Your first stop is The Great Wave of Kanagawa. A hush settles over the gallery as light glances off the cool surface of the print. Stand about three paces back from The Great Wave of Kanagawa, so the entire sweep of the wave and the tiny boats below come into view. From here, the tension between the towering crest and the distant Mount Fuji is unmistakable, and the fine lines of Hokusai’s carving reveal themselves with clarity—details easily lost if you’re too close.

Katsushika Hokusai, the most reproduced image in Japanese art, lived from 1760 to 1849, creating The Great Wave of Kanagawa during his lifetime. This iconic work was acquired by the Art Institute of Chicago, where it is displayed only three times a year. What you see before you is a yoko-e, or landscape-oriented, woodblock print. Created in late 1831, it measures about 25.7 by 37.9 centimeters. The Great Wave of Kanagawa—also called Under the Wave off Kanagawa—is part of Hokusai’s celebrated Thirty-Six Views, this renowned woodblock print from the series, of Mount Fuji series. The vivid blue wave dominates the foreground, its foamy claws curling over three fragile boats. The polychrome technique—layering multiple carved woodblocks inked with different pigments—allowed Hokusai to achieve the rich gradations of blue that have become so emblematic of this print. When Hokusai produced this work, he was in the later decades of his life. Years of personal upheaval and artistic reinvention had brought him to this point—seeking to capture not only the outward appearance of nature, but its overwhelming power and the vulnerability of those who venture into Thousands of copies of The Great Wave were originally produced and sold inexpensively, making it accessible to many during a period when Japanese trade was strictly controlled. The print balances awe and fear: the wave threatens to engulf, yet the boats press forward, and Fuji remains eternal. The Great Wave becomes a meditation on the relationship between humans and nature—fragile, persistent, and always at risk of being swept away.

Directions: Continue through Art Institute of Chicago — next is Paris Street; Rainy Day.

Stop 2: Paris Street; Rainy Day

Coordinates: 41.8781, -87.6298

Orientation: Stand a few paces back from Paris Street; Rainy Day, and let your eyes sweep across the full width of the canvas. From this position, the scale of the painting asserts itself: the figures and streetscape fill your field of view, and the relationship between the people, their umbrellas, and the vast, gridded city behind them becomes unmistakably present. It is here that the sensation of moving among strangers in the rain—at once connected and apart—unfolds most clearly.

Gustave Caillebotte inherited a fortune from his family's textile enterprise and real estate holdings, which gave him the freedom to pursue painting. In 1877, he completed this monumental canvas, capturing the massive urban transformation of Paris directed by Baron Georges-Eugène Haussmann. That same year, the work was first shown publicly at the Third Impressionist Exhibition in April.

Caillebotte’s decision to create Paris Street; Rainy Day as a large oil painting set it apart from many of his contemporaries. He chose oil on canvas for its depth and its ability to render subtle shifts of light and atmosphere. The painting’s scale and the careful arrangement of figures and architecture reflect his interest in perspective and the geometry of modern city life—a theme linked to the broader Impressionist interest in depicting contemporary existence. In this work, the city is not just a backdrop but a living environment. The surface of the painting, with oil paint laid down deliberately, captures the sheen of wet streets and the cool light of a rain-washed afternoon. The figures—some paired in conversation, others solitary—move through the city’s grid, echoing a sense of separation and fleeting connection.

Here, the emotional weight lies in the interplay of distance and intimacy: strangers brushing past, each shielded by an umbrella, each moving through the city’s rain.

Your final stop in Art Institute of Chicago: American Gothic.

Stop 3: American Gothic by Grant Wood

Coordinates: 41.8781, -87.6298

Orientation: As you stand here, position yourself slightly to the right of American Gothic by Grant Wood—just enough so the light from the gallery windows catches the texture of the paint on the beaverboard.

In 1930, American Gothic by Grant Wood was first exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago. As a result, American Gothic became one of the most iconic images in American art, solidifying its place in the Art Institute of Chicago's collection and in the broader cultural landscape. What you see before you is an oil painting created on beaverboard—a pressed wood fiber panel, not the traditional canvas. Grant Wood deliberately chose this material in 1930 to lend the work a certain solidity and texture, echoing the rugged resourcefulness of rural America in the midst of the Great Depression. The painting shows a stern-faced farmer, gripping his pitchfork, and a woman—often interpreted as his daughter—standing before a white, Carpenter Gothic-style house. Every element is sharply defined, almost severe. The quiet tension in their faces and posture suggests the weight of the era sits on their shoulders. From this vantage point, the painting captures a moment of rural endurance and pride with remarkable clarity, transforming into a powerful symbol. In 1930, Grant Wood drove through Eldon, Iowa, and spotted a farmhouse built with a striking Gothic lancet window. Intrigued by the contrast it created, Wood selected the building as his backdrop and titled his painting American Gothic in reference to its architectural style. To populate the scene, he recruited his dentist to pose as the farmer and used his own sister as a model, a decision that sparked family conflict between the painter and his sister.

This tour explores the interplay between human experience and the natural world, showcasing how artists like Hokusai and Grant Wood capture moments of vulnerability and resilience. These works invite us to reflect on our relationship with our surroundings and the enduring spirit of humanity in the face of change.

That's 3 stops in all.
